blocks.text:
How can I thank You, for all that is mine is Yours?
You have filled my home with every grace.
When Your light appeared, the darkness vanished.
Blessed is this day—Subhan Man Yarani!
It’s 4 a.m. on this cool Friday morning in Qadian. These beautiful verses by the Promised Messiah (as) echoed in my mind as I prepared for what promised to be a deeply spiritual and emotional day.

Mixed feelings overwhelmed me. It’s Friday—the most blessed day of the week—and we are in Qadian, the birthplace of Ahmadiyyat. What could be better? Alhamdulillah, we are all still healthy and in good spirits.

But today is also bittersweet as it marks our last full day in this blessed land. I recalled the accounts of companions of the Promised Messiah (as) describing how emotional their farewells to Qadian used to be. The Promised Messiah (as) would lovingly urge them to stay longer, and they would feel reluctant to leave. Today, we understand their feelings deeply. Like them, we have obligations—work, family, and school—that require us to return home.
Early Morning Devotion

Knowing this was our last day made us even more determined to make the most of it. Many of us rose early to spend time at the sacred sites within Darul Masih. We sought solitude with our Creator, thanking Him for granting us the opportunity to visit Qadian.

On my walk toward Masjid Aqsa, I passed by Darul Ziafat (Langar Khana). We had visited it the previous night and even had dinner there. The food we enjoyed at the Sarai was prepared here and sent over for us, while most other guests who come to Qadian eat their meals right at Darul Ziafat.

The admins there showed us the newly constructed "Q Wing," a section of the facility closest to Darul Masih. It is designated for VIP guests visiting Qadian and serves as a testament to the ever-growing hospitality of this sacred town. Reflecting on the dedication and seamless work of the volunteers and staff, I felt immense gratitude for everyone who ensures that Qadian remains a welcoming home for visitors from around the world.

The Langar Khana is more than just a kitchen—it is a living testament to the Promised Messiah’s (as) vision of serving humanity. Established during his lifetime, it has grown into a modern facility capable of producing thousands of meals daily. Its state-of-the-art Roti Plant can churn out countless flatbreads in minutes, meeting the needs of thousands of guests, particularly during Jalsa Salana.
A Gift of Knowledge and Exploration

At 8 a.m. sharp, the taxis were recalled for us, ready to take us on another round of exploration. Our guide, Naseer Haq Acharia Murabbi of Ammore Kharja, was there on time as ever with his welcoming smile, and Sadr Dibba Sahib joined us to oversee the day’s activities. Despite it being our last day in Qadian, the excitement to see more of this blessed town was evident in everyone.
We had two specific places on our agenda for the morning: the Roti Plant, which we hadn’t covered the previous day, and a return trip to the bookstore.

The Roti Plant was a remarkable experience. This state-of-the-art facility is a one-of-a-kind operation capable of producing thousands of rotis in minutes. It serves the ever-growing needs of the guests who visit Qadian, particularly during Jalsa Salana. Witnessing the efficiency of this plant, along with the dedication of those working there, was inspiring. It felt like a living example of how the Promised Messiah’s (as) vision of service continues to be fulfilled in the most practical and impactful ways.

After this, we made our way back to the Ahmadiyya Bookstore. Yesterday, the staff had stayed open just for us, but we hadn’t been able to browse as much as we wanted due to time constraints. Today, they once again graciously welcomed us, ensuring we had ample time to explore and purchase books.

The shelves were filled with beloved Ahmadiyya Islamic literature, all printed right here in Qadian at the Fazl-e-Umar Press. The excitement among us was palpable as we eagerly picked out books to take home—treasures of knowledge that would remind us of this spiritual journey and help us continue to grow in our faith.

We left the bookstore with bags full of books and hearts full of gratitude. Alhamdulillah, these moments were yet another testament to the blessings of Qadian. From there, we hurried back to prepare for Jumma, knowing that time in this sacred town was quickly slipping away.
A Special Moment: Calling the Adhan

My morning was more rushed than others’. I was preparing for a deeply personal and humbling experience—calling the Adhan for Jumma prayers at Masjid Aqsa. Jumma was scheduled for 1:15 p.m., and the first Adhan would be called at 12:45 p.m. I hurried to get ready and left for the masjid as others prepared for Jumma and began packing for our departure from Qadian.
My wish of calling the Adhan in Qadian was being fulfilled once again—and not just once, but thrice. Jumma prayers involve two Adhans, and I was assigned to call both.

Blessed is this day, the one in which I found my purpose.
Blessed is this day—Subhan Man Yarani!

As I stood in Masjid Aqsa waiting for the time, the realization of this moment struck me deeply. This wasn’t just about my voice echoing from the masjid—it was about being part of a spiritual legacy that connects us to the Promised Messiah (as).

The MTA Qadian team was present to capture parts of my Adhan at the masjid. Throughout our time in Qadian, MTA Qadian had been documenting our journey alongside Ghalib Ut-Hur Khan and Naem R. Mohamed from the USA. Their dedication to capturing these moments ensured that the memories of this trip would be preserved for generations to come.
An Afternoon of Reflection and Farewell

Jumma prayers at Masjid Aqsa were a deeply moving experience. The masjid was filled with the spiritual energy of hundreds of worshippers, united in prayer. After the khutba and prayers, we gathered for lunch at Sara-i-Waseem.

In the afternoon, many of us visited the Ahmadiyya Bookstore for the final time, purchasing keepsakes and beloved books printed at the Fazl-e-Umar Press. Others sought quiet moments of reflection, offering Nawafil at various sacred sites across Qadian.

This day felt like the culmination of everything we had experienced here—a blend of spirituality, history, and community. As the sun began to set, we prepared for our final evening in this sacred town, cherishing the memories and lessons we would carry with us forever.

Our hearts were getting heavier as the hours passed. We only had a few precious moments left in this sacred town, and I couldn’t help but feel the weight of the goodbye looming ahead. I didn’t want to leave, and I knew this was the sentiment shared by most of us.
The Friday Sermon

As evening approached, we headed back to Masjid Aqsa for combined Maghrib and Ishaa prayers. Huzur’s Friday Sermon, delivered live from London, UK, was scheduled for 6:30 p.m. Announcements were made, and members gathered in the masjid, filling the space with eager anticipation.

Huzur (aba) spoke on the topic of the Treaty of Hudaibiyah, capturing the rich history of Islam and the noble character of the Holy Prophet Muhammad (sa). He described the conditions of the treaty, the apprehension felt by Hazrat Umar (ra), and how the Holy Prophet (sa) dispelled the anxiety of the Muslims. His sermon was a profound reminder of patience, trust in Allah, and the wisdom of leadership. His words resonated deeply, serving as a timely reflection on the enduring lessons from Islamic history and the responsibilities we bear as members of the Jamaat.
A Look at Qadian’s Transformation

After the sermon, we were asked to remain in the masjid to watch a documentary on the renovation work in Qadian. The documentary was both informative and inspiring, showcasing the remarkable transformation of Qadian over the years.
The narration highlighted the revelation received by the Promised Messiah (as) in 1897:
Enlarge your abode. People will come to you from very distant lands.

The prophecy has been fulfilled in extraordinary ways. Qadian has undergone numerous renovations to accommodate the growing number of visitors. The most recent renovation project began in 2005, after the visit of Hazrat Khalifatul Masih V (aba). The documentary showed many before-and-after pictures of the buildings, and it was remarkable to see the transformation.

Almost every site we visited over the past three days was part of this massive effort. From the Langar Khana to the Masjid Aqsa, from the Roti Plant to the Ahmadiyya Bookstore, the renovations have preserved the historical significance of Qadian while modernizing it to meet the needs of today.
While watching, I realized the work is far from done. Qadian continues to grow and evolve under the guidance of Huzur (aba), preparing to welcome even more people from across the world.

After the documentary, we gathered for one last group photo in front of the Minaratul Masih. Standing together, we felt the weight of our collective gratitude and the bittersweet reality of bidding farewell. We said our goodbyes to Darul Masih, offering one last Salam to Masjid Mubarak and Masjid Aqsa. These sacred places, where so many prayers have been answered and where history was made, had become part of our hearts.
As we walked back to Sara-i-Waseem, the Minaratul Masih shone brightly behind us, a beacon of hope and a reminder of the incredible legacy of the Promised Messiah (as).
A Last Supper in Qadian

The food quality throughout our stay was nothing short of remarkable. Every single meal was delicious, prepared with love and care, and incredibly healthy. Over the entire trip, no one ever complained about getting sick after eating, nor did anyone grow tired of the food served at the dining hall. Each bite of roti and every dish prepared at Darul Ziafat seemed infused with thoughtfulness and effort, leaving us grateful for every meal.

The hospitality staff, mostly graduates of Jamia Ahmadiyya Qadian currently serving as murabbis, served us tirelessly. These students come not just from Qadian but from all over India and sometimes overseas. Their service was seamless, quiet, and filled with genuine affection. Tea always followed dessert, arriving just when needed. Their proactive care and love for the guests of the Promised Messiah (as) created an atmosphere that will be hard to forget.

During dinner, the air was thick with sadness. Many of us took the time to thank these gracious hosts who had been feeding and caring for us over the last few days. They served us selflessly, asking for nothing in return, and their kindness deeply touched us all.
A Special Encounter
I asked one murabbi if they liked Qadian as much as we did. To my surprise, he said, “We are sad when we have to go home for holidays. We cannot wait to return to Qadian.”

Later that evening, another murabbi from Kashmir shared a poignant moment with me. When I asked if he felt relieved when guests left Qadian, he paused and asked me which room I was staying in. It seemed unusual, but I told him.
That night, he knocked on my door with his phone in hand. On the screen was a nazm from Durr-e-Sameen by the Promised Messiah (as):

When guests come with love and affection,
It brings joy to the heart and comfort to my soul.
But when the time of farewell comes, it grieves the heart.
Blessed is this day—Subhan Man Yarani!

He said, “We love serving and helping the guests of the Promised Messiah (as). We feel honored that you have traveled from lands far away to visit this small village. But yes, we too feel sad when the time of farewell arrives.”
Our eyes welled up as we embraced. The moment was a testament to the bond of brotherhood that transcends borders, languages, and time.
It was time to finish packing and prepare for our early departure. Our buses would be ready by 5 a.m.

As we drifted off to sleep, our hearts were filled with gratitude for the countless blessings of this journey. May we carry this experience with us and let it inspire us to serve humanity and our Jamaat with renewed zeal.

title: Reflections on the Road Back Home

blocks.text: Sad. Tired. And reluctant to get up. It wasn’t because of fatigue; it was because we did not want to leave. But as the saying goes, every good thing must come to an end.

Asia, Europe, America, and Africa—I’ve seen them all,
But nowhere is there a place like Qadian.
The admins, Haris and Nabeel bhai, were busy getting everyone ready, but even they seemed weighed down by the sadness of departure.

Some of us may have risen early for one final prayer at Darul Masih. Perhaps a few quietly slipped out to Bahishti Maqbara for one last visit. I wouldn’t know, being a chaperone kept me occupied—ensuring not only that I packed everything but also helping others double-check their belongings.

The buses were loaded, and we said our final goodbyes. Standing together for one last congregational silent prayer, we asked Allah for His guidance and protection before we boarded the buses and left Qadian.
Our minds were already racing ahead to prepare for our journey back—Delhi Mosque, Delhi Airport, and eventually home. But there was no denying it: we had left our hearts behind in Qadian.

Once we roamed its streets,
Now the streets of Qadian roam before our eyes.
Reflections on the Journey

On the bus, one of our young Waqf-e-Nau members took on the role of MC, keeping the passengers entertained by asking general knowledge and Jamaat-related questions to teams. While some of us participated, others nodded off into naps—it was an eight-hour drive, after all.
For me, it was a mix of brief naps and deep reflection. What did this journey mean to me? What did it mean to visit these sacred sites in Delhi, Agra, and Qadian?

For more than three centuries, the Mughals ruled much of India, leaving behind architectural marvels such as the Red Fort and the Taj Mahal. But where are the Mughals now? Their marvels and their forts stand as relics of a bygone era. Ahmadiyyat, on the other hand, established in 1889, stands as an eternal legacy. And by the grace of Allah, it will endure forever.
We are here in India to refresh our faith in Islam and Ahmadiyyat, to see firsthand the legacy of the Promised Messiah (as), and to remind ourselves of the blessings we are part of.

People from all over the world visit various tombs, seeking history or grandeur. But it is the Promised Messiah’s grave in Bahishti Maqbara—and the graves of his companions—where people sincerely offer prayers and send Salam.
The Mughals built the Red Fort in Old Delhi to protect themselves from their enemies, but Allah revealed to Hazrat Promised Messiah (as):
I will save all who dwell in the House.

Was this revelation referring to the physical house of Darul Masih, to Qadian, or to Ahmadiyyat as a whole? Regardless, we all felt that we were within the fort of Allah, with our commanders being the Holy Prophet Muhammad (sa) and Hazrat Promised Messiah (as). No enemy can ever conquer this fort.

The Mughals had their Diwan-e-Khas and Diwan-e-Aam, grand halls for private and public gatherings. But can they compare to the humble rooms of Hazrat Amma Jaan or Hazrat Promised Messiah? What about the gatherings atop Masjid Mubarak, where revelations descended, or the Shah Nasheen at Bahishti Maqbara, where companions sat in the presence of the Promised Messiah?

The light of Minaratul Masih shines far brighter in our hearts than the lights and sounds of the Red Fort’s nightly show. To us, Minaratul Masih holds a meaning so profound that Qutub Minar pales in comparison.
And what of the Taj Mahal, a celebrated symbol of love? It cannot rival the stories of Hazrat Promised Messiah’s love for his Creator.

The Promised Messiah (as) was mortal in the love of Allah. In his own words, this meant dissolving his soul in the divine, becoming one with Allah in his worship and devotion. His entire being became a masjid, a sanctuary for Allah’s presence.

He was nicknamed Maseetar, someone who lives in the mosque, and at some point, he seemed to embody the essence of a mosque itself. Hazrat Promised Messiah (as) built Masjid Mubarak even though Masjid Aqsa was just a short walk away. He created Baitul Riazat, Baitul Dua, and Baitul Fikr—spaces dedicated to worship, prayer, and reflection. Who else looks for so many opportunities to connect with their Creator?

His love for the Holy Prophet Muhammad (sa) was unparalleled, and I’ve written about it in my diary before, so I’ll skip it here. But have you heard the stories of the Promised Messiah’s love for Hazrat Amma Jaan? Or the stories of his beloved companions?

The Taj Mahal, with all its grandeur, has nothing on Qadian. I am glad we saw these historical landmarks in Delhi and Agra, for they gave us a chance to compare and realize the true significance of what we have in Qadian.
Qadian is better than the Red Fort, Qutub Minar, and even the Taj Mahal. It’s not just history; it’s living proof of Allah’s grace and the fulfillment of His promises.
Carrying the Light Forward

We are the group of Waqf-e-Nau. The children in our group are the future leaders of our Jamaat. On this journey, we have lit our candles from the eternal light of Hazrat Promised Messiah (as). Our duty now is clear: to take this light and illuminate the entire world.

O my dear friends, do not rest until
The flag of Qadian waves over the entire world.
May Allah enable us to fulfill our responsibilities and make this journey a source of lasting blessings. Ameen.

It is often emphasized by our elders in the Jamaat that we should maintain a strong connection with Huzur, regularly writing to him and seeking his prayers. Building a personal relationship with the Khalifa is not only spiritually enriching but also a testament to the power of prayer. We’ve all heard stories of prayers being answered the moment a letter is written to Huzur—a living example of faith in Allah’s mercy and the blessings of Khilafat.
A Test of Faith at Delhi Airport

On Sunday, December 1, 2024, our Buffalo Group experienced firsthand the miracle of such prayers. After an incredible journey to Qadian, we arrived at Delhi Airport for our return flight with Air France at 6:30 am, connecting via Paris to Toronto.

What began as a routine check-in soon unraveled into a series of delays. The Air France flight was repeatedly postponed, causing concern among us. From my frequent travel experience, I suspected the delays might culminate in a cancellation. Anxiety grew within our group—children risked missing school, and several adults, including my co-chaperone Mohammad Ali Sahib and myself, had pressing work commitments waiting.

Sensing the gravity of the situation, I encouraged the children in our group to immediately write to Huzur. I submitted a letter through the Waqf-e-Nau website and contacted Mirza Haris Ahmad Sahib, Secretary Waqf-e-Nau USA. Haris Sahib assured me he would also write to Huzur on our behalf, and I prayed that Allah would pave the way for us.

As feared, the flight was ultimately canceled, plunging the airport into chaos. For two hours, it seemed impossible to find a solution. The Air France staff, who had been so efficient in Toronto, seemed overwhelmed and unorganized in Delhi. The prospect of being stranded in Delhi for 2–3 days loomed over us—a scenario we could not afford.

Throughout the ordeal, I remained in contact with Haris Sahib, Mirza Nabeel Sahib (our trip coordinator), and Hanan Khan Sahib (our travel agent). But despite their efforts, progress felt stagnant. At one point, doubt crept into my mind: How could writing to Huzur possibly change this dire situation?
A Divine Intervention

Yet, Allah’s miracles often come when we least expect them. While most passengers from our flight were sent to hotels to await rescheduled flights, our group remained at the airport. Out of nowhere, an exhausted Air France agent walked past us. I recognized her as someone I had seen being berated by frustrated passengers earlier.

Curious about our group, she stopped to hear about our situation. Initially, she seemed dismissive, treating it as just another complaint. But then, something changed. She asked to see our passports. Despite her clear fatigue after working over 24 hours, she carefully reviewed every passport and started rebooking us.

To our astonishment, she managed to book every member of our group onto an Air India flight leaving later that evening. Her extraordinary effort in the midst of her exhaustion felt nothing short of divine intervention.
We flew out that evening, arriving home by Monday morning. As we reflected on the experience, it was clear that Allah’s grace had been at work.
Staying Connected with Khilafat

Later, when I shared this story with Haris Sahib, he jokingly remarked that Huzur must have prayed so much for the Buffalo Group that week, given the series of letters he’d received about us. I could only respond with a heartfelt, “Alhamdulillah.”

This experience reminded me—and everyone in our group—that Allah is indeed a Living God. He continues to show His signs to those who seek Him. Staying connected with Khilafat is not just a recommendation; it is a lifeline.
Write to Huzur. Seek his prayers. Build your connection with Khilafat. In doing so, you too will witness the wonders of Allah’s guidance in your life.
Alhamdulillah, we returned safely to our homes, our hearts filled with gratitude, and our faith strengthened through this unforgettable experience.

title: A Sad News: The Last Dervish of Qadian

blocks.text: Today, we received solemn news: Respected Tayyib Ali Sahib, the last Dervish of Qadian, has passed away by the decree of Allah.
Indeed, to Allah we belong and to Him shall we return.

May Allah grant him forgiveness, elevate his ranks, and bestow upon him a high place in Paradise. Ameen, Thumma Ameen. May Allah accept the sacrifices of all the Darweshan and grant the next generation the ability to uphold their noble traditions.
The Caller is the Most Beloved; O heart, dedicate yourself to Him.
A Historical Context

In 1947, during the Partition of India, Muslims were moving to Pakistan, while Hindus and Sikhs relocated to India. Qadian, the birthplace of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community, remained in Indian Punjab.

Recognizing the significance of Qadian as the spiritual center of Ahmadiyyat, Hazrat Musleh Maud (ra), the Second Khalifa of the Promised Messiah (as), made a historic decision. He instructed 313 devoted individuals, later known as Darweshan-e-Qadian, to stay behind in Qadian. These Darweshan were tasked with safeguarding the sacred sites, protecting Jamaat properties, and preserving the spiritual heritage of Qadian during a time of great turmoil and uncertainty.

Their sacrifices were immense. They lived simple, selfless lives, enduring hardships and challenges with unwavering faith. Their dedication ensured that the birthplace of the Promised Messiah (as) remained a vibrant center of spirituality and history.
Meeting the Last Dervish

During our recent trip to Qadian (November 21—December 1, 2024), we had the honor of meeting Tayyib Ali Sahib. He was seated in a wheelchair near Darul Masih. Though frail with age, his presence was profoundly moving. He graciously allowed us to embrace him, shake his hand, and even take photographs with him.

It is humbling to think that he was a living connection to the sacrifices made during the turbulent times of partition. His unwavering commitment to the mission of the Promised Messiah (as) ensured that the legacy of Ahmadiyyat remained intact.
Reflections on the Darweshan

Most of the people we met during our time in Qadian—the shopkeepers, students, and Jamaat workers—are the children and grandchildren of these noble Darweshan. Their lives continue to embody the sacrifices and spirit of devotion passed down through generations.

As we reflect on Tayyib Ali Sahib’s passing, we are reminded of the enormity of the responsibility these individuals carried. They were not just custodians of property; they were guardians of history, culture, and the mission of the Promised Messiah (as).
With Tayyib Ali Sahib’s passing, an era has come to an end. Yet, the legacy of the Darweshan lives on in the hearts of Ahmadis worldwide.
Long live Qadian.
Long live the legacy of Darweshan-e-Qadian.
Dear friends,

When I started writing, my goal was simple: to take all of you along on this journey, even if you couldn’t physically be with us. It’s been a privilege to share these experiences, and I hope they brought Qadian and its blessings a little closer to your hearts.
Along the way, I’ve received so much love, encouragement, and helpful advice. I’m truly grateful for all of it. Thank you for following along and for your kind words.

Of course, there were some stories and inside jokes I couldn’t include, and there might be moments I missed that were important to you. Please forgive me for any omissions. Feel free to message me if there’s something you’d like me to know or share.
Please keep me and my family in your prayers. May Allah bless you all and grant us the opportunity to undertake such journeys again.
With love and gratitude,
Anas Mangla
